\chapter{Una queja}
\label{ch:es-una-queja}
\hlchaptermodality{665}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can complain about damage or a problem, ask for the manager or the owner and ask to be compensated.}

Complete the last lesson of chapter 665: I can complain about damage or a problem, ask for the manager or the owner and ask to be compensated.

\section[la queja]{la queja — the complaint}

\label{lesson:ES-C665-queja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the socket, then the Spanish for the tap.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la queja}
\textbf{la queja} — \textquotedblleft{}the complaint\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tengo una queja sobre el ruido.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I have a complaint about the noise.}
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{quejarse}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{queja} is built on \emph{quejarse} \textquotedblleft{}to complain\textquotedblright{}, which is usually traced to a Vulgar Latin form of \emph{quassāre} \textquotedblleft{}to shake hard, to batter\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la queja}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la queja}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la queja}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the socket, then the Spanish for the tap, then say \emph{la queja} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la queja mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The complaint\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el desperfecto]{el desperfecto — the minor damage, the defect}

\label{lesson:ES-C665-desperfecto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the tap, then the Spanish for the complaint.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el desperfecto}
\textbf{el desperfecto} — \textquotedblleft{}the minor damage, the defect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La habitación tenía varios desperfectos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The room had several things damaged.}
\end{quote}

Small damage: a broken lamp, a stain on the wall.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desperfecto} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{perfecto} \textquotedblleft{}perfect\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{perfectus} \textquotedblleft{}finished\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{perficere}, built on \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desperfecto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el desperfecto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el desperfecto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the tap, then the Spanish for the complaint, then say \emph{el desperfecto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el desperfecto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The minor damage, the defect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[compensar]{compensar — to compensate, to make up for}

\label{lesson:ES-C665-compensar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the complaint, then the Spanish for the minor damage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: compensar}
\textbf{compensar} — \textquotedblleft{}to compensate, to make up for\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El hotel nos compensó con una noche gratis.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The hotel made up for it with a free night.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Compensar a alguien por algo} — to compensate someone for something.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{compensar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{compēnsāre} \textquotedblleft{}to weigh things against one another, to balance\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short; EtymDB), built on \emph{pēnsāre} \textquotedblleft{}to weigh\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{compensar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{compensar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{compensar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the complaint, then the Spanish for the minor damage, then say \emph{compensar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does compensar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To compensate, to make up for\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el gerente]{el gerente — the manager}

\label{lesson:ES-C665-gerente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the minor damage, then the Spanish for to compensate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el gerente}
\textbf{el gerente} — \textquotedblleft{}the manager\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quiero hablar con el gerente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I want to speak to the manager.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la gerente}, sometimes \emph{la gerenta}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gerente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{gerēns, gerentis} \textquotedblleft{}managing\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{gerere} \textquotedblleft{}to carry on, to manage\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el gerente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el gerente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the minor damage, then the Spanish for to compensate, then say \emph{el gerente} again

\section[el dueño]{el dueño — the owner}

\label{lesson:ES-C665-dueno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to compensate, then the Spanish for the manager.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el dueño}
\textbf{el dueño} — \textquotedblleft{}the owner\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El dueño del hostal es muy simpático.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The owner of the guesthouse is very nice.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la dueña}. \emph{El dueño del perro} — the owner of the dog.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dueño} is inherited from Late Latin \emph{domnus}, a short form of Latin \emph{dominus} \textquotedblleft{}master\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{domus} \textquotedblleft{}house\textquotedblright{}: the master of the house.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el dueño}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to compensate, then the Spanish for the manager, then say \emph{el dueño} again
